title: The Unquiet Cipher
premise: Kestrel Sterling, the reclusive coroner of Hollow Creek, receives two letters on the same morning: one confessing to a murder Kestrel closed years ago, and one promising that more will follow unless a hidden ledger is found. As bodies begin surfacing with ciphered marks, Kestrel realizes the town's founding families encoded their debts and crimes in gravestone inscriptions they've walked past all their lives. The trail leads to Kestrel's own missing mother, whose disappearance was the first entry in the ledger. In the end, Kestrel must choose between exposing the truth that will destroy their found family of townsfolk or burning the ledger and letting the dead keep their silence—choosing truth at last, but at the cost of everything familiar.
about_author: T. M. Delacroix is the pen name of a former mortuary records clerk who spent a decade in small-town offices where everyone knew everyone's business. They write mysteries about quiet places that keep loud secrets.

chapters.title: Two Envelopes, One Morning
chapters.summary: Kestrel Sterling's POV. Opening the office on an ordinary Tuesday, Kestrel finds twin letters in the mail slot—one confessing to the Marlow drowning case Kestrel closed three years ago, one promising 'the rest of the ledger' if Kestrel looks closely. The emotional beat is unease: Kestrel's carefully invisible life has been noticed by someone who knows too much.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Walking the cemetery to steady themselves, Kestrel notices fresh chalk rubbings taken from old headstones—founding-family markers from the 1890s. Deputy Ada Reyes reports the same names appearing in a vandalism report. The beat is creeping dread as Kestrel realizes someone is reading the stones like text.

chapters.title: The Confession That Doesn't Fit
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, with a flashback to the Marlow case. Re-examining the drowning file, Kestrel finds the confession letter's details match evidence never made public—but the confessed killer died two winters back. The beat is vertigo: either a living person fed him the details, or Kestrel closed the wrong case.

chapters.title: Ada Reyes Knows Something
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Kestrel and Ada. Ada covers for a gap in her patrol log the night the second letter arrived; Kestrel notices but says nothing, testing loyalty against suspicion. The beat is the first fracture in trust between the town's two most honest people.

chapters.title: A Body With Marginalia
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A drifter washes up at Miller's Bend with a string of numbers tattooed inside his wrist—numbers matching dates in the cemetery's oldest plot. The beat is cold clarity: this isn't harassment anymore; it's a body count beginning.

chapters.title: The Ledger Hidden in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Cross-referencing gravestone epitaphs with birth and death dates, Kestrel discovers a substitution cipher: the stones record payments, debts, and names never written in any church book. The beat is exhilaration curdling into horror—the founders were laundering something darker than money.

chapters.title: What Mother Left Behind
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, intimate and raw. Searching their late childhood home, Kestrel finds their mother's handwriting matching the second letter's script—and a half-burned page listing her own name as a ledger entry dated the week she vanished. The beat is grief reopened after twenty years.

chapters.title: The Founders' Descendants
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV chapter rotating through four prominent families. Each descendant privately admits knowing fragments—a locked box, a whispered warning, a payment still collected annually. The beat is complicity: the whole town is built on a shared refusal to look down.

chapters.title: Second Body, Same Cipher
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The church organist is found dead in the crypt, positioned beside the ledger's key stone, a chalk rubbing clutched in her hand. She had called Kestrel twice and hung up both times. The beat is guilt—Kestrel ignored the warnings because answering meant being seen.

chapters.title: Ada's Night Off
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Flashback reveals Ada was paid anonymously years ago to lose a file—her sister's medical debt erased in exchange for silence about a car at Miller's Bend. The beat is shame and self-justification: survival has a price, and she's been paying it quietly ever since.

chapters.title: The Man Who Collects
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Following the annual payment trail, Kestrel confronts Elias Vann, the funeral director, who admits he's the courier—not the author. He passes along a message: 'Your mother wrote both letters before she went into the ground. Or didn't.' The beat is whiplash hope: she may be alive.

chapters.title: Exhumation
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, procedural tension. Kestrel legally exhumes the grave bearing their mother's name and finds it empty except for a tin box containing the ledger's decoding key—and a third letter, decades old, addressed to whoever finally dug. The beat is devastating patience rewarded: she planned for this.

chapters.title: The Key Turns
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Decoding fully, Kestrel learns the ledger records not just debts but disappearances—people the founding families erased, including witnesses to a 1970s fire that killed six mill workers. The beat is righteous fury hardening into resolve: these aren't secrets, they're crimes still breathing.

chapters.title: Someone Burns the Archive
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The county records annex burns overnight; Ada is first on scene and recognizes accelerant patterns she was once paid to ignore. The beat is escalation—the enemy is inside the town's institutions and moving faster than Kestrel can decode.

chapters.title: Loyalty Priced Out
chapters.summary: Dual POV, Kestrel and Ada. Ada confesses everything to Kestrel—her bribe, her silence, her fear. Kestrel must decide whether the woman who covered for the enemy can be trusted to stand with them now. The beat is forgiveness offered without certainty, loyalty chosen over safety.

chapters.title: The Empty Plot at Midnight
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A note lures Kestrel to the cemetery at midnight; instead of their mother, they find the surviving Vann patriarch dying of a self-inflicted dose, whispering that he 'kept her comfortable' for twenty years—in the old sanatorium wing. The beat is dread transformed into direction.

chapters.title: Sanatorium Wing C
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Ada's POV alternating. Breaking into the sealed wing, they find a woman living quietly among records—older, sharp, unmistakably Kestrel's mother, who faked her death to become the ledger's living custodian. The beat is reunion shadowed by betrayal: she let Kestrel grieve to keep them safe.

chapters.title: Why She Stayed Buried
chapters.summary: Mother's POV, long withheld. She explains: the ledger's final page names the last living founder—the beloved retired judge who signed off on the mill fire cover-up—and every custodian who moved against him died. The beat is terrible inheritance: finishing the ledger means becoming its next target.

chapters.title: The Judge's Dinner
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Invited to the judge's annual founders' dinner, Kestrel attends armed only with copies, watching the town's finest toast their history while knowing what's under the frosting. The beat is controlled terror—Kestrel publicly promises to close one more case, and watches the judge understand.

chapters.title: Miller's Bend, Rising Water
chapters.summary: Climax, Kestrel and Ada POV. The judge corners Kestrel at the flood-prone bend where the Marlow man really died; Ada arrives with backup she spent twenty years afraid to call. In the rising water and rain, the confession letters' true author is revealed: the judge himself, taunting Kestrel into leading him to the key. The beat is mortal stakes and moral clarity colliding.

chapters.title: Reading the Names Aloud
chapters.summary: Falling action, ensemble POV. The judge is arrested; the decoded ledger is read aloud at a town meeting, name by name, while descendants weep or deny. Kestrel's mother chooses to stay in Hollow Creek, alive under her real name. The beat is catharsis—truth spoken together costs less than truth carried alone.

chapters.title: New Stones, Old Ground
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, epilogue. Months later, Kestrel carves new markers for the ledger's forgotten dead and adds their mother's name—living—to the town roll. A final letter arrives, unsigned: 'Some ledgers never close.' Kestrel smiles, files it, and locks the office. The beat is earned peace with open eyes: survival's price was paid, and it was worth it.
